prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "SPACE EXPLORATION TECHNOLOGIES CORP" (ticker SPCX). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt, revenue growth, operating margin, short interest, institutional ownership, revenue growing faster than expenses, 5-year return vs the S&P 500, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent. Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: SpaceX is close to an ideal Rule Breaker: the top dog and first mover in reusable rockets and satellite broadband, a visionary founder in Elon Musk, early backing from investors such as Founders Fund and Google, a famous consumer brand in Starlink, and a stock many commentators call overvalued at about 92 times sales. The weaker trait is recent price momentum, as the shares at $156.54 are up about 16% from the $135 IPO price but well below the $225.64 high of June 2026.
summaries.buffett: Buffett would admire SpaceX's moat in low-cost launch and Starlink, but it is a newly public, loss-making company (net loss of about $4.94B in 2025) with no long public record, heavy capital spending on AI and Starship, and a founder with about 85% of the voting power. At a market value of about $2.1 trillion, there is no margin of safety on his terms.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise the rare engineering achievement and cost advantage behind Falcon 9 and Starlink, but inverting raises many ways to lose: Starship delays, the loss-making xAI/X segment, key-person risk around Musk, and a valuation that already assumes enormous success. It would likely go in his 'too hard' pile.
summaries.lynch: SpaceX is a fast grower (recast revenue up from $10.39B in 2023 to $18.67B in 2025), but its story now mixes rockets, satellite internet and an AI lab, which is harder to sum up simply. It has no earnings for a P/E-to-growth test, it is one of the most hyped stocks on Wall Street, and the June 2026 IPO greatly increased the share count.
summaries.fisher: SpaceX fits Fisher's growth points unusually well: a long sales runway in broadband, launch and AI compute, relentless new product development (Starship, Starlink V3, direct-to-cell), R&D that has produced world-leading products, and a strong sales record with over 10 million Starlink customers. The weaker points are thin, volatile profitability and governance concentrated in one founder.
summaries.graham: SpaceX fails nearly all of Graham's defensive criteria: it has no long public earnings record, lost money in 2025, pays no dividend, and trades at about 16 times book value with no positive trailing earnings. It is large, but its valuation is far outside Graham's limits.
summaries.thiel: SpaceX, in which Thiel's Founders Fund invested early, answers most of his seven questions strongly: reusable rockets give a step-change cost advantage, the timing for satellite broadband was right, it started with a niche (commercial launch) and expanded, it has an exceptional founder and its own distribution, and its position looks durable. Few companies match his 'zero to one' model as closely.
summaries.gerstner: SpaceX rides several trends Gerstner looks for, global connectivity, space and AI compute, with consensus expecting FY2026 revenue of about $45B, more than double 2025. The question for Gerstner would be price: about 99 times forward earnings and heavy AI capital spending leave little room for disappointment.
summaries.druckenmiller: SpaceX has a very strong growth trajectory (H1 2026 revenue up 54%), clear catalysts such as Starship and Starlink V3 launches and AI compute contracts like Anthropic's, and estimates that have risen with new deals. Against that, the stock has fallen from its June high, profits are negative, and its liquidity and lock-up dynamics as a new IPO add risk.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would like Starlink's high margins (a segment operating margin of about 39% in 2025), but SpaceX as a whole is loss-making, burns cash because capital spending far exceeds operating cash flow, and is priced at about 92 times sales. It fails his 'good company' test on returns and his 'don't overpay' test on price.
summaries.greenblatt: SpaceX cannot rank on the Magic Formula because it has an operating loss, giving a negative return on capital and earnings yield. It would be excluded from a Greenblatt screen.
summaries.akre: SpaceX has a strong business in launch and Starlink and a long reinvestment runway, two good signs for Akre. But returns on capital are negative overall because of AI and Starship spending, and governance is concentrated in Elon Musk, so the stool is not balanced.
summaries.pabrai: SpaceX is the opposite of a Dhandho bet: there is no distress, the outcome is highly uncertain, and at about $2.1 trillion the downside could be large if growth falls short. Pabrai's approach of buying simple businesses cheaply would not apply.
summaries.wood: SpaceX is close to the centre of ARK's research: it leads in reusable rockets and satellite broadband, owns xAI's Grok and Colossus AI compute, and its falling launch costs open up new markets such as orbital data centers. It combines several innovation platforms and its addressable market, which the S-1 puts at over $28 trillion, could expand many times.
summaries.ackman: SpaceX has a dominant, high-barrier franchise in launch and Starlink, but it is not simple or predictable today: it is loss-making, capital-intensive and controlled by its founder, leaving shareholders little influence. Ackman's preference for predictable free cash flow bought at a discount is not met at today's price.
summaries.sleep: SpaceX is a strong 'scale economies shared' business: cheaper reusable launches let it deploy more satellites, and Starlink has cut prices (ARPU fell from $99 to $66 a month) while growing to 10.3 million subscribers. Its position in 10-20 years looks likely to be stronger, though the AI segment adds uncertainty Sleep might dislike.
summaries.valentine: SpaceX solves huge problems (expensive access to space and lack of internet in remote places) in very large markets, the kind Don Valentine prized. Its technology-driven, market-creating profile fits his approach well, though as a $2 trillion public company it is far beyond the venture stage.
summaries.nash: SpaceX scores well on Nash's qualitative steps (a founder CEO, a wide moat, secular trends in space, connectivity and AI) and reaches 85 on the scorecard. It fails the quantitative ones: free cash flow is deeply negative (-$32.5B trailing), operating margin is about -15%, and no DCF with its own history comes close to its $2.1 trillion value.

momentum.evidence: SpaceX listed on June 12, 2026 at $135 and closed at $156.54 on Oct 13, 2026 (+16%), but it is well below its $225.64 high of June 16 and traded around $113.50 in late July.

g4.evidence: It is led by founder Elon Musk and was backed before its IPO by well-known investors such as Peter Thiel's Founders Fund, Google and Fidelity.

g6.evidence: At about 92 times trailing sales and a $2.1 trillion market value, the stock is widely called overvalued, for example by Argus, which warned of a multi-year re-rating risk.

simple.evidence: Rockets and satellite internet are easy to grasp, but the mix of launch, Starlink, Starship R&D, xAI and X makes the combined business hard to value.

b2.evidence: Recast revenue grew from $10.39B (2023) to $18.67B (2025), but results before 2023 were never published and it swung from a $466M operating profit in 2024 to a $2.6B operating loss in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Musk has been consistent about the Mars mission and the S-1 disclosures are detailed, but he holds about 85% of voting power and his pay is tied to his own goals such as a Mars colony.

b6.evidence: Merging in Musk's xAI and X in 2026 brought a segment that lost $6.4B at the operating level in 2025, which looks like empire-building across Musk's companies.

roic.evidence: The company had an operating loss in 2025 and a trailing operating margin of about -15% (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), so its return on capital is negative despite profitable Starlink.

fcf.evidence: Capital spending far exceeds operating cash flow, with $15.8B of AI capital spending in Q2 2026 alone, so free cash flow is deeply negative.

b10.evidence: SpaceX has only traded publicly since June 2026, so there is no long record to compare retained earnings with market value created.

safety.evidence: At $156.54 the shares trade at about 92 times sales and 16 times book value with no trailing profit, far above any conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: Even with consensus FY2026 revenue growth of about 143%, a forward P/E of about 99 and a $2.1 trillion value price in many years of success.

mu5.evidence: With about $100.0B of cash and securities in June 2026 and Starlink's strong economics, outright failure is unlikely, but Starship setbacks, AI losses or a Musk-related crisis could badly hurt value.

reinvest.evidence: Starlink earned a segment operating margin of about 39% in 2025 and can absorb huge investment, but returns on the AI and Starship spending are unproven.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower, but the story now combines launch, satellite broadband and an AI lab rather than one simple theme.

ly3.evidence: SpaceX has a trailing loss of $2.27 per share, so the P/E test cannot be met.

runway.evidence: Starlink subscribers grew from 4.4M (2024) to 10.3M (March 2026) and it is adding direct-to-cell, aviation, maritime and AI compute markets.

ly7.evidence: The share count rose about 42% over the past year with the June 2026 IPO, and there is no record of insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Its June 2026 IPO drew worldwide attention and dozens of analysts (38 in the S&P Global consensus) now cover it.

fi2.evidence: As Falcon 9 matured SpaceX developed Starlink, Starship, Starlink V3 satellites and direct-to-cell service.

fi3.evidence: Its engineering produced the first reusable orbital rockets (about 650 Falcon launches with a 99%+ success rate) and the largest satellite network, with 9,600+ Starlink satellites.

fi4.evidence: It wins most commercial launches worldwide, sold Starlink in about 164 countries and signed airlines such as United and Qatar Airways.

longterm.evidence: SpaceX spends heavily on Starship and Mars goals that will take years to pay off, accepting a 2025 operating loss.

gr1.evidence: It had $18.67B of 2025 revenue and a market value of about $2.1 trillion in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: SpaceX reported a net loss of about $4.94B in 2025, and audited results before 2023 were never published.

eps10.evidence: No per-share earnings history before its 2026 IPO is available to measure ten-year EPS growth.

gr6.evidence: It has a trailing net loss, so the price is not covered by average earnings at all.

gr7.evidence: With negative trailing earnings and a P/B of about 16, it cannot meet the 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Reusable Falcon 9 boosters, flown over 85% of the time on reused hardware, give SpaceX a cost per kilogram rivals cannot approach, and it carried over 80% of the world's mass to orbit in 2025.

timing.evidence: Cheap launch arrived just as demand for global broadband, direct-to-cell service and AI compute exploded.

th3.evidence: It started by winning a large share of the small commercial-launch and NASA cargo markets and expanded into Starlink broadband and crew flights.

team.evidence: Founder Elon Musk and President Gwynne Shotwell have led SpaceX from three failed Falcon 1 launches to about 170 launches in 2025.

th5.evidence: Starlink sells directly online and through retailers, airlines, shipping firms, governments and mobile carriers such as T-Mobile.

durable.evidence: Its decade-long lead in reusability and vertical integration, and thousands of satellites in orbit, should be hard to dislodge in 10-20 years, though Amazon and Chinese networks are coming.

th7.evidence: SpaceX pursued rocket reuse when the industry considered it uneconomic, and built a satellite network others did not believe could pay.

trend.evidence: It leads the commercial space economy and global satellite connectivity, and rents AI compute to customers such as Anthropic.

dr1.evidence: Revenue rose 54% in H1 2026 and consensus FY2026 revenue is about $45B, but losses have widened with AI spending (trailing net loss of about $8.9B).

dr2.evidence: Starship-launched Starlink V3 satellites and new AI compute contracts could make it much stronger by 2028, but much of this is already in analysts' FY2027 revenue estimate of about $117B.

dr4.evidence: Demand for broadband and AI compute is strong, but a capital-hungry company priced on long-term growth is sensitive to interest rates and market liquidity.

dr6.evidence: Starship reaching operational orbit, Starlink V3 deployment, direct-to-cell expansion and new AI compute contracts are clear upcoming catalysts.

dr7.evidence: The franchise is exceptional, but heavy losses, a $2.1 trillion value and key-person risk make a large concentrated position risky.

gm.evidence: Gross margin improved from about 41% in 2023 to about 49% in 2025, high for a hardware and telecom business.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield is negative (about -1.5% per StockAnalysis, Oct 2026) because capital spending far exceeds operating cash flow.

gb2.evidence: SpaceX had an operating loss over the trailing twelve months, so operating profit relative to its roughly $2.06 trillion enterprise value is negative.

pa2.evidence: The shares are about 30% below their June 2026 high and the AI segment is loss-making, but the core launch and Starlink businesses are not in a setback.

pa4.evidence: The business is unlikely to fail given $100.0B of cash and securities, but at about 92 times sales a permanent loss on the shares is possible if growth disappoints.

wo1.evidence: SpaceX owns xAI (Grok, Colossus AI data centers) and leads in reusable rockets and satellite connectivity.

wo2.evidence: Reusable boosters have sharply cut the cost to orbit, and Starlink has cut prices (ARPU from $99 to $66 a month) as subscribers grew to 10.3 million.

wo3.evidence: It combines reusable rockets, satellite networks and AI compute, with plans to link them through orbital data centers.

wo4.evidence: Its S-1 claims a total addressable market above $28 trillion, and Starlink and AI compute could grow its revenue many times in five years.

ac3.evidence: It does not depend on commodity prices, but it relies on US government contracts (about a fifth of 2025 revenue), regulation and capital markets to fund heavy spending.

ns1.evidence: SpaceX uses its launch scale to lower Starlink prices and keep Falcon 9 cheaper than rivals, which makes it ever harder for competitors to catch up.

ns4.evidence: If Starship and Starlink V3 succeed, its cost advantage and network will be much larger in 10-20 years than today.

va2.evidence: It solves the high cost of reaching space and the lack of fast internet for billions of people in remote areas, on ships and on planes.

tn1.evidence: SpaceX was built from 2002 for the commercial space economy and now sells infrastructure (launch, Starlink connectivity and AI compute) into secular trends in space, broadband and AI.

tn2.evidence: The popular story is a rocket company, while most revenue now comes from Starlink connectivity and it is adding AI compute through xAI, but at about 90 times sales the market already prices in much of that shift.

tn3.evidence: SpaceX is a US mega cap founded in 2002, outside small caps, Chinese companies, commodities, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups, though it has only been listed since June 2026.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew from $10.39B (2023) to $18.67B (2025) and cash of $100,009M exceeded debt of $39,708M at June 30, 2026, but it is not profitable (Q2 2026 net loss $541M).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was negative in every reported quarter (-$9,067M in Q1 2026 and -$15,963M in Q2 2026), and debt exceeded cash in March 2026 ($30,603M vs $23,675M).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 33.2% in 2025 to $18.67B and 91.9% year on year in Q2 2026 to $7,814M.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth is strong (33.2% in 2025), but trailing free cash flow of -$32.52B on $23.04B of revenue (StockAnalysis) gives a deeply negative score.

tn8.evidence: In H1 2026 revenue rose 53.7% to $12,508M but costs before operating income rose 64.9% to $14,603M, although Q2 2026 alone showed revenue rising faster than costs.

tn9.evidence: It fails the instant kill of an operating margin below 20% (about -15% trailing), though it now passes on market cap, net cash, short interest (7.07% of float) and age.

tn10.evidence: Regulatory and legal probes of Grok and X, FAA launch licensing for Starship and spectrum and landing-rights rules for Starlink are ongoing risks, though none currently threatens the core business.

tn11.evidence: SpaceX provides launch services, Starlink satellite internet and AI computing that help governments, companies and households reach orbit and get broadband anywhere, and charges per launch, monthly subscriptions and compute contracts; customers choose it because reusable rockets make it the cheapest and most reliable option.

tn13.evidence: Total 85: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest 5 (7.07% of float), institutional ownership 5 (25.75%), revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return 0 (listed June 2026), moat 10, CEO 10, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 10, talent 10.

tn14.evidence: SpaceX has no five-year public record: results before 2023 were never published, it had an operating loss in 2025 and free cash flow is negative.

tn15.evidence: Assets excluding goodwill are 2.76x liabilities ($181,125M / $65,546M), the current ratio is 5.12 and liabilities are 0.52x equity, but interest coverage is negative because of the operating loss (June 30, 2026).

tn18.evidence: Founder Elon Musk has run SpaceX since 2002 with a historic execution record and owns a large stake, but there are no open-market purchases, and SpaceX was private until June 2026.

tn20.evidence: SpaceX has reported only one quarter as a public company (Q2 2026, revenue $7.8B vs about $6.9B expected and a smaller-than-expected loss), too few to judge consistency.

tn21.evidence: It is not free of red flags: the 2026 merger with Musk's own xAI and X looks like an acquisition by a related party, operating margins fell to about -15% as AI spending grew, and Musk is a polarising CEO.

tn22.evidence: It has real revenue ($23.04B trailing) and a strong core, but it has weak current fundamentals (net losses, -$32.52B trailing FCF), raised cash in a June 2026 IPO and attracts nonstop media hype.

tn24.evidence: With negative free cash flow, the $2.08T market value implies many years of very fast growth and a large margin swing, far beyond what the company is delivering today.

tn25.evidence: Its 3-year average free-cash-flow margin is negative, so Nash's DCF gives no positive operating value; even $60.3B of net cash is only about $4.57 per share (13,182M shares), far below $156.54.

tn26.evidence: As an unprofitable grower its price to trailing sales is about 90 (StockAnalysis, Oct 14, 2026), far above aerospace and telecom peers, and no meaningful PEG exists.
